Bill Text
The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2.
The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices heard in the political process and hold their elected officials accountable.
(b) Elections for local or state elective office should be fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can force candidates to rely on large contributions from wealthy donors and special interests, which can give those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine the public’s trust that public officials are performing their duties in an impartial manner and that government is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents than challengers because they seek access to elected officials, and such contributions account for a large portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as confirmed by studies such as those published in the Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which qualified candidates can receive
public funds for the purpose of communicating with voters rather than relying exclusively on private donors, are currently operative in five charter cities in California, as well as numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage competition by reducing the financial advantages of incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy donors or special interests, to run for office, as confirmed by studies such as those published in State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the State Politics and Policy
Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit improper practices, protect against corruption or the appearance of corruption, and protect the political integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public money reduces rather than increases the fund raising pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces the undue influence of special interest groups.”
(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United States Supreme Court recognized that “public financing as a means of eliminating
the improper influence of large private contributions furthers a significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564 U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court acknowledged that public financing of elections “can further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme Court further noted that citizen-funded elections programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign financing allows special interests to gain disproportionate influence and unfairly
favors incumbents. An exception should be created to permit citizen-funded election programs so that elections may be conducted more fairly.
SEC. 3.
Section 85300 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85300.
(a) A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
(b) Candidates shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be utilized to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not, at any time, use public funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after their campaign ends, use any source of funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Available candidate funds” means the candidate’s expenditure limit or the sum of all contributions and public funds received by the candidate’s controlled committee for the elective office, whichever is less.
(2) “Expenditure limits” means voluntary spending limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must abide by to receive public funds.
(3) “Independent expenditures against” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in opposition to a specific candidate.
(4) “Independent expenditures in support” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in support of a specific candidate.
(5) “Net supportive funds” means the sum of available candidate funds,
plus the independent expenditures in support of that candidate, minus the independent expenditures against that candidate.
(6) “Public funds” means any moneys provided to a candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the purpose of seeking elective office.
(7) (A) “Strict criteria” means the requirements set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. These criteria shall require candidates to demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents.
(B) (i) If a statute, ordinance, or charter requires a
minimum number of individuals making small-dollar contributions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the largest contribution the statute, ordinance, or charter may require for a contributor to be counted is ten dollars ($10).
(ii) For purposes of this subparagraph, a statute, ordinance, or charter may allow a contribution larger than the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A) to be counted as a contribution equal to the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A).
(C) “Strict criteria” shall not include requirements that candidates receive a specified number of signatures or raise a specified total dollar amount of more than ten dollars ($10) per contributor.
(f) (1) A statute, ordinance, or charter may increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(2) An increased limit pursuant to this subdivision shall not exceed an amount equal to the highest dollar amount of net supportive funds of any other candidate for the same office, plus the dollar amount of independent expenditures against the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate, minus the dollar amount of independent expenditures in support of the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(g) Public funding statutes, charters, ordinances, and resolutions shall not discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent.
(h) The Commission is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
(i) Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this section may be amended only by a statute that complies
with subdivision (b) of Section 81012.
SEC. 4.
Section 85320 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85320.
(a) A foreign government or foreign principal shall not make, directly or through any other person, a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(b) A person or a committee shall not solicit or accept a contribution from a foreign government or foreign principal in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(c) For the purposes of this section, a “foreign principal” includes the following:
(1) A foreign political party.
(2) A person outside the United States, unless either of the following is established:
(A) The person is an individual and a citizen of the United States.
(B) The person is not an individual and is organized under or created by the laws of the United States or of any state or other place subject to the jurisdiction of the United States and has its principal place of business within the United States.
(3) A partnership, association, corporation, organization, or other
combination of persons organized under the laws of or having its principal place of business in a foreign country.
(4) A domestic subsidiary of a foreign corporation if the decision to contribute or expend funds is made by an officer, director, or management employee of the foreign corporation who is neither a citizen of the United States nor a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States.
(d) This section shall not prohibit a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure made by a lawfully admitted permanent resident.
(e) (1) Any person who violates this section shall be guilty of a misdemeanor.
(2) In addition to other
penalties, a person who violates this section shall be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding an amount equal to three times the amount contributed or expended.
SEC. 4.1.
Section 85320 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85320.
(a) A foreign government, foreign principal, or foreign national shall not make, directly or through any other person, a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(b) A person
or a committee shall not solicit or accept a contribution from a foreign
government, foreign principal, or foreign national in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(c) For the purposes of this section, the following terms have the following meanings:
(1) (A) “Foreign national” means a person who is not a citizen of the United States and who is not a lawfully admitted permanent resident.
(B) “Foreign national” does not include a person who has been granted deferred action, and whose deferred action has not expired, under the federal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, as described in guidelines issued by the United States Department of Homeland Security.
(2) “Foreign principal” includes any of the following:
(A) A foreign political party.
(B) A person outside the United States, unless either of the following is established:
(i) The person is an individual and a citizen of the United States.
(ii) The person is not an individual and is organized under or created by the laws of the United States or of any state or other place subject to the jurisdiction of the United States and has its principal place of business within the United States.
(C) A partnership, association, corporation, organization, or other combination of persons organized under the laws of or having its principal place of business in a foreign country.
(D) A domestic subsidiary of a foreign corporation if the decision to contribute or expend funds is made by an officer, director, or management employee of the foreign corporation who is neither a citizen of the United States nor a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States.
(d) This section shall not prohibit a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure made by a lawfully admitted permanent resident.
(e) (1) Any person who violates this section shall be guilty of a
misdemeanor.
(2) In addition to other penalties, a person who violates this section shall be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding an amount equal to three times the amount contributed or expended.
SEC. 5.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any provision of this act or its application is held invalid, that invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application.
SEC. 6.

(b) Notwithstanding Section 9040 of the Elections Code or any other law, the Secretary of State shall, pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 81012 of the Government Code,

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
SB 42, Umberg.
Political Reform Act of 1974: public campaign financing: California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974, prohibits a public officer from expending, and a candidate from accepting, public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office.
This bill would remove prohibitions imposed on a public officer or candidate to expend or accept public funds, as defined, for the purpose of seeking elective office unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety. The bill would require candidates to abide by specified expenditure limits and meet strict criteria, as defined, to qualify for public funds. The bill would prohibit public funds from being used to pay
legal defense fees or fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign. The bill would permit a statute, ordinance, or charter to establish standards to increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate pursuant to a specified formula. The bill would provide that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not responsible for administering or enforcing a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
Existing law prohibits a foreign government or foreign principal, as defined, from making a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the
election of a candidate to state or local office. Under existing law, a person who violates this prohibition is guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to a fine equal to the amount contributed or expended.
This bill would instead require that a person guilty of
that misdemeanor, in addition to other penalties, be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding a maximum amount of 3 times the amount contributed or expended.
The Political Reform Act of 1974, an initiative measure, provides that the act may be amended by a statute that becomes effective upon approval of the voters.
This bill would require the Secretary of State to submit the provisions of the bill, as specified, to the voters for approval at the November 3, 2026, statewide general
election. This bill would incorporate additional changes to Section 85320 of the Government Code proposed by AB 953 to be operative pursuant to specified conditions.

The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2.
The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices heard in the political process and hold their elected officials accountable.
(b) Elections for local or state elective office should be fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can force candidates to rely on large contributions from wealthy donors and special interests, which can give those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine the public’s trust that public officials are performing their duties in an impartial manner and that government is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents than challengers because they seek access to elected officials, and such contributions account for a large portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as confirmed by studies such as those published in the Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which qualified candidates can receive
public funds for the purpose of communicating with voters rather than relying exclusively on private donors, are currently operative in five charter cities in California, as well as numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage competition by reducing the financial advantages of incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy donors or special interests, to run for office, as confirmed by studies such as those published in State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the State Politics and Policy
Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit improper practices, protect against corruption or the appearance of corruption, and protect the political integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public money reduces rather than increases the fund raising pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces the undue influence of special interest groups.”
(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United States Supreme Court recognized that “public financing as a means of eliminating
the improper influence of large private contributions furthers a significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564 U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court acknowledged that public financing of elections “can further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme Court further noted that citizen-funded elections programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign financing allows special interests to gain disproportionate influence and unfairly
favors incumbents. An exception should be created to permit citizen-funded election programs so that elections may be conducted more fairly.
SEC. 3.
Section 85300 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85300.
(a) A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
(b) Candidates shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be utilized to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not, at any time, use public funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after their campaign ends, use any source of funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Available candidate funds” means the candidate’s expenditure limit or the sum of all contributions and public funds received by the candidate’s controlled committee for the elective office, whichever is less.
(2) “Expenditure limits” means voluntary spending limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must abide by to receive public funds.
(3) “Independent expenditures against” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in opposition to a specific candidate.
(4) “Independent expenditures in support” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in support of a specific candidate.
(5) “Net supportive funds” means the sum of available candidate funds,
plus the independent expenditures in support of that candidate, minus the independent expenditures against that candidate.
(6) “Public funds” means any moneys provided to a candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the purpose of seeking elective office.
(7) (A) “Strict criteria” means the requirements set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. These criteria shall require candidates to demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents.
(B) (i) If a statute, ordinance, or charter requires a
minimum number of individuals making small-dollar contributions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the largest contribution the statute, ordinance, or charter may require for a contributor to be counted is ten dollars ($10).
(ii) For purposes of this subparagraph, a statute, ordinance, or charter may allow a contribution larger than the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A) to be counted as a contribution equal to the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A).
(C) “Strict criteria” shall not include requirements that candidates receive a specified number of signatures or raise a specified total dollar amount of more than ten dollars ($10) per contributor.
(f) (1) A statute, ordinance, or charter may increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(2) An increased limit pursuant to this subdivision shall not exceed an amount equal to the highest dollar amount of net supportive funds of any other candidate for the same office, plus the dollar amount of independent expenditures against the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate, minus the dollar amount of independent expenditures in support of the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(g) Public funding statutes, charters, ordinances, and resolutions shall not discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent.
(h) The Commission is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
(i) Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this section may be amended only by a statute that complies
with subdivision (b) of Section 81012.
SEC. 4.
Section 85320 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85320.
(a) A foreign government or foreign principal shall not make, directly or through any other person, a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(b) A person or a committee shall not solicit or accept a contribution from a foreign government or foreign principal in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(c) For the purposes of this section, a “foreign principal” includes the following:
(1) A foreign political party.
(2) A person outside the United States, unless either of the following is established:
(A) The person is an individual and a citizen of the United States.
(B) The person is not an individual and is organized under or created by the laws of the United States or of any state or other place subject to the jurisdiction of the United States and has its principal place of business within the United States.
(3) A partnership, association, corporation, organization, or other
combination of persons organized under the laws of or having its principal place of business in a foreign country.
(4) A domestic subsidiary of a foreign corporation if the decision to contribute or expend funds is made by an officer, director, or management employee of the foreign corporation who is neither a citizen of the United States nor a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States.
(d) This section shall not prohibit a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure made by a lawfully admitted permanent resident.
(e) (1) Any person who violates this section shall be guilty of a misdemeanor.
(2) In addition to other
penalties, a person who violates this section shall be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding an amount equal to three times the amount contributed or expended.

SEC. 5.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any provision of this act or its application is held invalid, that invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application.

1. The actual text of SB 42 — specifics of Section 85300.
2. The No campaign funding — who's behind it (quick guide says no contributions reported to No on 4 campaign). Interesting: the opposition is taxpayer groups without money, while Yes campaign... let me check contributions to Yes on 4.
3. The claim about county central committee candidates — is it accurate?
4. Notable splits: SF Chronicle against, LA Times for, McClatchy for, San Diego Union-Tribune against, Mercury News against, Press Enterprise against, Santa Cruz Sentinel neutral.
5. Prior history: 2000 Prop 25? Actually the 2000 measure was "Proposition 25"? CalMatters says "Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising." That was Prop 26? Let me check. And 2010 Proposition 15 — "Public Campaign Funding Act" — 58% opposed.

Wait, but 2010 Prop 15 was an initiative statute that would have lifted the ban and created a voluntary program. It failed with 42% yes, 58% no. That's a relevant data point: even with a fully specified program, voters said no.

Hmm, that's important context: In 2010, Prop 15 was a well-designed, limited measure (only for the Board of Equalization and voluntary, funded by lobbyist fee) — and voters rejected it 58-42.

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 18, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. It does cap one thing: a program may raise a participating candidate's spending limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, but only up to a formula in the text, the highest "net supportive funds" of any other candidate in the race plus outside spending against the participating candidate, minus outside spending for them.

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
SB 42, Umberg.
Political Reform Act of 1974: public campaign financing: California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974, prohibits a public officer from expending, and a candidate from accepting, public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office.
This bill would remove prohibitions imposed on a public officer or candidate to expend or accept public funds, as defined, for the purpose of seeking elective office unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety. The bill would require candidates to abide by specified expenditure limits and meet strict criteria, as defined, to qualify for public funds. The bill would prohibit public funds from being used to pay
legal defense fees or fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign. The bill would permit a statute, ordinance, or charter to establish standards to increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate pursuant to a specified formula. The bill would provide that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not responsible for administering or enforcing a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
Existing law prohibits a foreign government or foreign principal, as defined, from making a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the
election of a candidate to state or local office. Under existing law, a person who violates this prohibition is guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to a fine equal to the amount contributed or expended.
This bill would instead require that a person guilty of
that misdemeanor, in addition to other penalties, be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding a maximum amount of 3 times the amount contributed or expended.
The Political Reform Act of 1974, an initiative measure, provides that the act may be amended by a statute that becomes effective upon approval of the voters.
This bill would require the Secretary of State to submit the provisions of the bill, as specified, to the voters for approval at the November 3, 2026, statewide general
election. This bill would incorporate additional changes to Section 85320 of the Government Code proposed by AB 953 to be operative pursuant to specified conditions.

The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2.
The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices heard in the political process and hold their elected officials accountable.
(b) Elections for local or state elective office should be fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can force candidates to rely on large contributions from wealthy donors and special interests, which can give those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine the public’s trust that public officials are performing their duties in an impartial manner and that government is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents than challengers because they seek access to elected officials, and such contributions account for a large portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as confirmed by studies such as those published in the Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which qualified candidates can receive
public funds for the purpose of communicating with voters rather than relying exclusively on private donors, are currently operative in five charter cities in California, as well as numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage competition by reducing the financial advantages of incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy donors or special interests, to run for office, as confirmed by studies such as those published in State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the State Politics and Policy
Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit improper practices, protect against corruption or the appearance of corruption, and protect the political integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public money reduces rather than increases the fund raising pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces the undue influence of special interest groups.”
(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United States Supreme Court recognized that “public financing as a means of eliminating
the improper influence of large private contributions furthers a significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564 U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court acknowledged that public financing of elections “can further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme Court further noted that citizen-funded elections programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign financing allows special interests to gain disproportionate influence and unfairly
favors incumbents. An exception should be created to permit citizen-funded election programs so that elections may be conducted more fairly.
SEC. 3.
Section 85300 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85300.
(a) A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
(b) Candidates shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be utilized to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not, at any time, use public funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after their campaign ends, use any source of funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Available candidate funds” means the candidate’s expenditure limit or the sum of all contributions and public funds received by the candidate’s controlled committee for the elective office, whichever is less.
(2) “Expenditure limits” means voluntary spending limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must abide by to receive public funds.
(3) “Independent expenditures against” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in opposition to a specific candidate.
(4) “Independent expenditures in support” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in support of a specific candidate.
(5) “Net supportive funds” means the sum of available candidate funds,
plus the independent expenditures in support of that candidate, minus the independent expenditures against that candidate.
(6) “Public funds” means any moneys provided to a candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the purpose of seeking elective office.
(7) (A) “Strict criteria” means the requirements set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. These criteria shall require candidates to demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents.
(B) (i) If a statute, ordinance, or charter requires a
minimum number of individuals making small-dollar contributions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the largest contribution the statute, ordinance, or charter may require for a contributor to be counted is ten dollars ($10).
(ii) For purposes of this subparagraph, a statute, ordinance, or charter may allow a contribution larger than the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A) to be counted as a contribution equal to the small-dollar contribution amount required pursuant to subparagraph (A).
(C) “Strict criteria” shall not include requirements that candidates receive a specified number of signatures or raise a specified total dollar amount of more than ten dollars ($10) per contributor.
(f) (1) A statute, ordinance, or charter may increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(2) An increased limit pursuant to this subdivision shall not exceed an amount equal to the highest dollar amount of net supportive funds of any other candidate for the same office, plus the dollar amount of independent expenditures against the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate, minus the dollar amount of independent expenditures in support of the qualified, voluntarily participating candidate.
(g) Public funding statutes, charters, ordinances, and resolutions shall not discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent.
(h) The Commission is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
(i) Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this section may be amended only by a statute that complies
with subdivision (b) of Section 81012.
SEC. 4.
Section 85320 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85320.
(a) A foreign government or foreign principal shall not make, directly or through any other person, a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.
(b) A person or a committee shall not solicit or accept a contribution from a foreign government or foreign principal in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the election of a candidate to state or local office.

(2) In addition to other
penalties, a person who violates this section shall be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding an amount equal to three times the amount contributed or expended.

Compiled by California Today from the text of Proposition 4 (SB 42, Chapter 245 of 2025), the Legislative Analyst's analysis and the Assembly Elections Committee analysis of SB 42 (July 2, 2025). Dollar amounts, contribution matches and spending limits are not set by Proposition 4; each program would set its own.
The Fair Political Practices Commission would advise on Prop 4 programs but would not enforce local ones:
The FPPC, which enforces the Political Reform Act today, gets a limited role. The text says the commission "is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency." The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm) expects state and local officials to ask the commission how to design programs that fit the new rules, which "likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff." The FPPC told the Legislature it would need one attorney at a cost of $205,000 in the first year and $198,000 a year after that, according to the Assembly Elections Committee's analysis of SB 42 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/media/2586), and noted possible additional enforcement costs.
The measure also splits how its own rules can be changed later. The definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC clause can be amended by the Legislature under the Political Reform Act's usual standard, a two-thirds vote in each house for a change that furthers the act's purposes. Every other part of the new section 85300, including the earmark exclusion and the ban on using public funds for fines and loan repayment, could be changed only with voters' approval.
Prop 4 also amends section 85320, the state's ban on contributions and spending by foreign governments, foreign principals and foreign nationals in state and local elections. Violating it is a misdemeanor today with a fine equal to the amount given or spent. Under Prop 4 the fine would be at least that amount and up to three times it. The committee analysis notes that this misdemeanor, unlike the act's general criminal penalty, does not require proof that a violation was knowing or willful.
California's ban on public campaign funds dates to Proposition 73 in 1988:
The ban came out of a head-to-head contest. In June 1988, voters faced two initiatives that would have rewritten campaign finance law in opposite directions. Proposition 68 offered contribution limits and state matching funds for legislative candidates who accepted spending limits. Proposition 73 offered contribution limits and a flat prohibition: "No public officer shall expend and no candidate shall accept any public money for the purpose of seeking elective office." Both passed, Prop 68 with 52.8% and Prop 73 with 58%, according to the Secretary of State's records (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/approval-percentages-initiatives.pdf). Because they conflicted, the California Supreme Court held in 1990 that only the measure with more yes votes could take effect, and Prop 68 was voided.
Federal courts later struck down Prop 73's contribution limits, but the public-funding ban survived. In 2000, voters approved Proposition 34, a Legislature-written campaign finance measure whose title promised contribution limits "Without Taxpayer Financing"; its ballot argument told voters that "our tax money is better spent on schools, roads and public safety."
The ban has one large exception. In 1992, in Johnson v. Bradley, the California Supreme Court upheld a Los Angeles charter measure that partly funded campaigns for city office, under the home-rule provision of the state Constitution. A 1990 appellate ruling held that the ban still applies to charter counties. The result, as the Assembly Elections Committee summarized it, is that "general law cities, all counties, all districts, and the state government are covered by the current ban," while charter cities can fund campaigns if they choose.
Three earlier measures to lift California's public financing ban failed between 2000 and 2010:
Each earlier attempt bundled the repeal with a specific program. Proposition 25 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2000-primary/sum_measures.pdf) in March 2000 would have publicly funded campaign advertising and voter information for candidates and ballot committees that accepted spending limits; it drew 34.7%. Proposition 89 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2006-general/measures.pdf) in November 2006 would have created a public financing system for candidates for state office; it drew 25.7%, the lowest of the three. Proposition 15 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2010-primary/ssov/ballot-measures-summary.pdf) in June 2010, placed on the ballot by the Legislature, would have run a public financing pilot for Secretary of State races; it drew 42.7%.
Prop 4 is built differently. It asks voters only to remove the ban and set conditions, and it leaves the decision to start a program, and how to pay for it, to each government.
SB 1107's 2016 attempt to lift the ban without a vote was struck down in court:
The Legislature has tried to remove the ban without a statewide vote before. In 2016 it passed SB 1107, by Senator Ben Allen, and Governor Jerry Brown signed it. The bill rewrote section 85300 to allow public funding when a government set up a dedicated fund open to all qualified candidates regardless of party or incumbency. Because Prop 73 had made the ban part of the voter-approved Political Reform Act, the Legislature could amend it without a vote only if the change furthered the act's purposes, and SB 1107 declared that it did.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and former Senator Quentin Kopp, one of Prop 73's proponents, sued. A Sacramento judge invalidated the law, and on August 26, 2019 the Third District Court of Appeal affirmed (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) the judgment, finding that SB 1107 "directly conflicts with a primary purpose and mandate of the Act, as amended by subsequent voter initiatives, to prohibit public funding of political campaigns." The judgment bars the FPPC from enforcing it. SB 1107's wording stayed in the code, but the FPPC continues to enforce the ban. Prop 4 deletes that wording and replaces it, which is why it needs voters' approval to take effect.
Two earlier versions of the current measure, AB 270 and SB 24 in the 2023–24 session, died in the appropriations committees. SB 42 was introduced on December 5, 2024 and passed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) the Senate 28–10 on June 2, 2025. The Assembly passed it 59–20 on September 12, the Senate concurred 29–8 the next day, and Newsom signed it on October 2 as Chapter 245 of the Statutes of 2025.
Los Angeles, San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland already fund campaigns under the charter-city exception:
The Assembly Elections Committee counts at least seven charter cities with public financing programs: Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, Richmond, Sacramento and San Francisco, though Richmond's and Sacramento's were not funded for recent elections. Most use matching funds, where the city multiplies small contributions from residents. Oakland's voters chose vouchers instead.
Four California charter cities fund campaigns with public money:
City Program and origin How candidates qualify What candidates can receive
Los Angeles Matching funds, enacted by city voters At least 100 contributions of $5 or more from district residents, at least $12,857 in qualified contributions, a $40,000 cap on self-funding, spending limits and a debate or town hall (2024 council rules) $6 for every $1 of a qualified contribution, matched up to $129 per donor; up to $174,000 in the primary and $217,000 in the general for a council candidate (2024)
San Francisco Public financing, created by Proposition O in November 2000 Supervisor candidates who are not incumbents need 100 resident contributions of $10 to $100 totaling $10,000; mayoral candidates who are not incumbents need 500 totaling $50,000; spending limits and three debates An initial grant, then $6 for every $1 raised; up to $255,000 for supervisor and $1.2 million for mayor (incumbents slightly less)
Berkeley Berkeley Fair Elections Act, approved by voters in 2016 At least 30 contributions of $10 or more from Berkeley residents totaling at least $650; a $60 cap on any one contribution and no loans (2026 rules) $6 for every $1 on contributions of up to $60; capped at $52,000 for City Council and $155,000 for mayor
Oakland Democracy Dollars, created by Measure W in November 2022 Candidates who opt in can collect vouchers from residents Each eligible resident gets $100 in vouchers to assign; the program is not funded for 2026 and is being prepared for 2028, with a limited public financing program in place for 2026
Compiled by California Today from the Los Angeles City Ethics Commission's 2024 Matching Funds FAQ, the San Francisco Ethics Commission's program overview, Berkeley's 2026 Public Financing Program guide and the Oakland Public Ethics Commission's Democracy Dollars page. Long Beach, Richmond and Sacramento have also enacted programs; the Assembly Elections Committee reports Richmond's and Sacramento's were not funded for recent elections.
San Francisco's program shows what one of these costs. City law requires a General Fund appropriation of $2.75 per resident each year into the Election Campaign Fund, capped at a $7 million balance. In the November 2024 mayoral and supervisorial races, the program paid out a record $8,840,187 to 27 candidates, $4.1 million of it to four mayoral candidates, according to the San Francisco Ethics Commission's post-election report (https://sfethics.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/2025.03.14-Agenda-Item-6-2024-Post-Election-Report.pdf). The same report found that outside groups spent $19.0 million on those races, also a record. Oakland shows the other side of the ledger: voters approved its $100-per-resident Democracy Dollars (https://www.oaklandca.gov/Government/Boards-Commissions/Public-Ethics-Commission/Democracy-Dollars-Program) program in November 2022, and the city has not funded it for 2026.
Proposition 4 costs the state a few hundred thousand dollars a year and leaves program costs to local choices:
The LAO's estimate covers only the state's direct cost: the FPPC's added legal staff, "much less than one-tenth of 1 percent" of the General Fund. Anything larger depends on what governments do afterward. "The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them," the analysis says, and "the total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed." Prop 4 does not require any government to create a program, and it does not say where the money would come from beyond excluding the three earmarked categories.
The two sides frame that open question differently. The Yes argument says that if a community adopts a program, "the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year." San Francisco law sets aside $2.75 per resident a year. The No argument says the measure "has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive"; the text indeed sets no dollar amount and leaves it to each program, which must also impose spending limits on the candidates it funds.
The Prop 4 campaign has raised $235,157 with no opposition committee:
Prop 4 is one of the quietest campaigns on the ballot. The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-4-sb-42-umberg-political-reform-act-1974-public-campaign-financing-california-fair-elections-act-2026-ch-245-2025), which runs through October 6, lists one committee, Movement Voter PAC's committee supporting Prop 4, with $235,157, and "No committees identified" in opposition. No committee on either side has raised the $1 million that puts it on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), last updated October 14. The Voter Information Guide lists the Yes campaign as Californians for Fair Elections, sponsored by Government Reform Advocates, and the No contact as the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments on Proposition 4 split over special-interest money and taxpayer cost:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Catherine Kennedy of the California Nurses Association and Senator Umberg, is headed "Elections should be won, not bought." It says "more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone" since 2020, that "thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems," and that Prop 4 "does not create a public financing program." Its rebuttal adds that "California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns."
The argument against, signed by former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, former FPPC commissioner Colleen McAndrews and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says the measure "allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns." It says Prop 4 sets "NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get," quotes the measure's definition of strict criteria to argue that "there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria," and says candidates "can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too." Its rebuttal, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and Schnur, points to "more than 60 candidates" for governor in the June primary. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
The guide's index lists the League of Women Voters, the California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works and Consumer Watchdog as supporters, and the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action as opponents. In its letter to the Legislature, the California Taxpayers Association also raised a First Amendment objection, arguing that taxpayers "would be forced to finance political speech they do not wish to support."
Campaign voices on both sides have made the same points to reporters. Trent Lange, president of the California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes campaign, said candidates should be able "to run and win without having to raise big money," and Dora Rose of the League of Women Voters said Prop 4 "sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence," CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-4-explainer/). Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, said on the Assembly floor that "the voters have been quite clear they don't want taxpayer money being used for politics." CalMatters also cites a National Conference of State Legislatures count of 15 states and Washington, D.C. with some form of statewide public financing, and describes the research on whether such programs reduce donors' influence as mixed.
Proposition 4 trails 42% to 53% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 42% yes, 53% no and 5% undecided, making Prop 4 one of the weakest measures on the ballot. Republicans oppose it 78% to 19% and independents 54% to 41%, while Democrats support it 55% to 39%. Self-described liberals back it 62% to 34%. Renters split 50% yes to 48% no while homeowners oppose it 55% to 39%, and households earning under $40,000 lean yes, 50% to 46%. One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 35% yes and 35% no with the rest undecided. PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom included a yes on Prop 4 in the ballot slate he announced on October 9. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) opposes it. Among editorial boards, the Sacramento Bee recommends yes and the San Diego Union-Tribune, the Orange County Register and the San Francisco Chronicle recommend no, according to CalMatters' roster (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/). The Chronicle argued that the measure's rules "are only meaningful if they're enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be." The Union-Tribune called Prop 4's "only certain effect" the creation of "a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for."
Proposition 4 after November 3 would hand the public financing decision to each government:
If Prop 4 passes, nothing changes on election day. The ban would end for the state, counties, general law cities and special districts, and any of them could then propose a program through its own statute, ordinance or charter, deciding the matching rate or voucher amount, the spending limits and the budget, within the measure's conditions. The FPPC would field questions, and a local program would be policed by whatever body that government sets up. Charter cities that already run programs would keep them. If it fails, the 1988 ban stays in place outside charter cities, as it has through three earlier repeal attempts and one struck-down law.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the text of SB 42 (Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025), campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State) and October 14, 2026 (FPPC), party and candidate positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–20, 2026.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?

That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Prop
4
CA
Prop
4
|
Statute
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
Repeals the ban on public financing of campaigns and allows state or local governments to establish programs that provide candidates with public funding under preestablished spending limits and eligibility requirements.
SPUR's Recommendation
California campaigns are expensive and donor-dependent. Public financing brings in more small-dollar donors, lowers barriers for first-time and under-resourced candidates, and increases candidate diversity and voter engagement. These benefits align with SPUR’s view that equitable representation requires campaign finance reform. Financing programs would add costs and create administrative burden, but because governments would opt in to Prop. 4, they would retain flexibility over whether and how to implement it. SPUR supports clearing this state-level barrier and letting cities, counties, and the state decide for themselves.
Vote YES
What Prop. 4 Would Do
Proposition 4 would give state and local jurisdictions the option of creating a public financing program for candidates running for office. If state and local governments opt in, they would have to develop spending limits and criteria for candidates to qualify for public funds. Candidates would be barred from using public finance dollars for legal defense fees, fines, or to repay personal loans to a campaign. The source of funding, such as a city’s General Fund or a property tax, is left to local governments, but the funds cannot come from money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
The Backstory
California has one main law governing campaign finance. In 1974, Proposition 9 created the Political Reform Act. This act regulates campaign finance disclosure, contributions, expenditures, lobbying practices, and government conflicts of interest and ethics. It has been amended more than 200 times. In 1988, Proposition 73 banned public campaign funding on the grounds that too much money was being spent on political campaigns and that public funds should be directed to other priorities.
Since then, several ballot measures have attempted to reshape the state’s public financing landscape with varying success. Proposition 34, passed in 2000, imposed contribution, transfer, and voluntary spending limits for candidates listed in the ballot pamphlet that remain largely in effect today. In 2016, the Legislature passed a measure that would have lifted the state’s ban on public financing, but the courts ruled that it needed to go to the voters. The legislature addressed this issue in 2025, resulting in Prop. 4 on the 2026 ballot.
Wealthy donors and corporate-funded political ads often dominate elections in California, sidelining everyday voters and eroding public trust in government. Lobbying groups spent more than $500 million to influence the state government in 2024, the most ever. 1 Prop. 4 does not set a limit on this activity but aims to help level the playing field by providing public funding to candidates who do not have access to support from wealthy individuals or corporations.
Campaigns have become increasingly expensive to run at all levels. At the state level, according to the organization Common Cause, it costs roughly $1 million to run and win a California Assembly seat and $1.7 million to run and win a State Senate seat. 2 As a result, megadonors and outside interests routinely foot the bill and, in the process, discourage those without wealthy networks from running.
Current state law permits public campaign financing only in charter cities, not at the state level or in non-charter cities. Of California's 121 charter cities, 6 have public financing programs: Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, Richmond, and San Francisco. Nationally, 20 other cities and counties and 14 states have public campaign financing. Public financing programs vary from grants and vouchers to matching programs. Los Angeles and San Francisco have a 6:1 matching fund — every $1 donated by a resident is matched by $6 from the city — with a cap depending on the office a candidate is running for. Seattle and Oakland offer Democracy Dollars, whereby every resident over 18 receives four $25 vouchers to donate to their preferred local candidate(s).
