Evidence suggests public campaign financing can lead to more small-dollar donors, greater donor diversity, and a broader range of people running for office. A 2022 University of Washington study found that in the two election cycles since Seattle implemented its program, the number of donors per race increased by 350%. Donations of less than $200 increased by 270%, and the number of candidates rose by 86% . A separate analysis also found that some residents were almost 12 times more likely to vote if they participated in the program, and low-income Seattleites and people of color were more likely to use their vouchers than they were to give a cash donation. 4
The Government Accountability Office's review of five programs (Arizona, Los Angeles, Minnesota, Montgomery County, Maryland, and Seattle) found that publicly financed candidates performed better than candidates who did not opt in. A participating candidate won or advanced in at least 50% of all contests in four of the five locations — reaching 85% to 95% in some Minnesota and Los Angeles elections. In matching-fund and voucher programs, candidates consistently received far more, but smaller, contributions; for example, in Los Angeles's 2022 mayoral race, publicly financed candidates averaged around 6,600 contributions of about $530 each, while non-participants averaged approximately 560 contributions of almost $25,000 each.
Prop. 4 was placed on the ballot legislatively through Senate Bill 42 (2025) and requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Wealthy, often demographically narrow donor networks currently dominate California campaign funding, disproportionately affecting people by race, income, and geography. Oakland’s 2023 campaign finance measure (Measure W) was proposed to address this disparity. Research found that campaign contributions gave disproportionate power to donors outside Oakland and in the city's wealthier, whiter neighborhoods. 5 That disproportionate power muted the political voice of lower-income residents and communities of color in their own local elections.
Public financing can counter such impacts. In Seattle, low-income residents and people of color were more likely to use Democracy Dollars than to make a cash donation, meaning the model activates participation among populations least engaged by traditional, wealth-dependent giving. Voucher users were also substantially more likely to vote. By lowering the fundraising bar, public financing also opens pathways for candidates without wealthy networks (often candidates of color, women, and working-class candidates) to run competitively, diversifying who’s on the ballot, not just who funds them. Prop 4 could encourage more candidates to run for office and help the candidate pools better reflect local racial, gender, and socioeconomic diversity. 6
Because Prop. 4 is optional for cities, these equity gains depend on which jurisdictions adopt and properly fund programs (as the research on Oakland’s still-unfunded Measure W shows). But removing the state-level barrier allows every California city and county to build systems that broaden who can run and whose voices matter locally.
Pros
Prop. 4 could encourage more candidates to run for office who reflect California’s racial, gender, and socioeconomic diversity by lowering the barrier to entry for candidates without wealthy networks, name recognition, or fundraising experience.
The measure would foster more small donors and reduce reliance on big money.
Public campaign financing can increase voter engagement and turnout when using vouchers.
The measure would allow local flexibility and would be optional, rather than a mandate, reducing the risk of a one-size-fits-all system.
Cons
Evidence on whether public campaign financing can reduce big-money influence in elections is mixed. Prop. 4 would not limit campaign financing through independent expenditures and political action committees, which have had outsized influence on elections since the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision.
Prop. 4 would present a cost to taxpayers. Public financing requires ongoing public money through General Fund appropriations, dedicated taxes, or fees.
The measure would entail administrative burden and complexity. Campaign financing programs require qualification review, spending-limit enforcement, audits, fraud detection, and other processes.

Public financing is the most effective counter we have to the influence of megadonors in politics.
Celina Avalos Jaramillo (https://www.brennancenter.org/about/staff/celina-avalos-jaramillo)

This November, California voters will decide whether to adopt Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm), a ballot measure that would allow the state to enact public campaign financing programs. Approving the measure would be a powerful way to counter the corrupting influence of big money in state politics. It would allow candidates to run competitive campaigns without depending on large donors and help more Californians engage meaningfully with the political process.
California elections are awash in money. In the 2026 primary elections, outside groups representing some of the state's wealthiest individuals and most powerful business interests spent $9 million (https://www.loscerritosnews.net/2026/05/29/money-floods-ad-67-race-9-million-in-outside-spending-turns-local-assembly-contest-into-proxy-war/) to influence just one assembly district seat. Several billionaires and billionaire-fueled PACs poured (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/01/tech-billionaires-california-elections) millions into other state legislative races that in the past would have been community-focused contests. These developments mirror a larger national trend in which a handful of ultra-wealthy donors increasingly dominate election spending. And this year's midterms are on track (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) to break spending records, with the top 50 donors (https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/interactive/2026/06/25/these-are-biggest-individual-donors-2026-election-cycle/) already having poured nearly $1.8 billion into the election. That figure doesn't include an additional reported $276 million (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-midterms.html) spent by Elon Musk.
Thanks to Citizens United and other court decisions, states and localities cannot limit how much billionaires and wealthy industries like AI, crypto, and hedge funds spend on California elections. But they can provide alternative ways for candidates to reach voters.
One of the most powerful is to provide voluntary public financing for candidates who have demonstrated viability. Public financing programs currently exist (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/guide-public-financing-programs-nationwide) in at least 14 states and 26 localities, including five California charter cities, but state law (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/about-fppc/about-the-political-reform-act/) currently bans other localities and the state from creating similar programs. Prop 4 would repeal that ban, giving the legislature and local governments the opportunity to create new public financing programs.
They would have a number of models to choose from. One of the most effective and best-studied systems is small donor matching, which matches small donations from individuals in the community with public funds. Los Angeles (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/), Berkeley (https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/elections/campaign-finance), Long Beach (https://library.municode.com/ca/long_beach/codes/municipal_code?nodeId=TIT2ADPE_CH2.01THLOBECAREAC), and San Francisco (https://sfethics.org/guidance/campaigns/candidates/public-financing-program) use this model, as do New York State and New York City. Other programs, including statewide systems in Arizona, Connecticut, and Maine, offer qualifying candidates block grants. Another model provides eligible voters with vouchers that they can use to assign public funds to participating candidates, as Oakland (https://www.oaklandca.gov/Government/Boards-Commissions/Public-Ethics-Commission/Democracy-Dollars-Program) will soon do. Prop 4 does not require the state or any locality to adopt any of these systems, or to enact public financing at all. It simply gives them the option.
Some who oppose (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php) Prop 4 argue that California's existing public financing programs need further study before expanding the reform in the state. But Prop 4 does not create any new programs - it simply gives the state and localities more options. Jurisdictions across the state that want to implement public financing would still be able to weigh the pros and cons while looking to especially strong models, like New York State, as they develop their own programs.
The benefits of public financing in New York and elsewhere are in fact well-documented. Data from New York State's first cycle (https://pcfb.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2025/01/2024-new-york-state-public-campaign-finance-board-election-cycle-report-final.pdf) of public financing in 2024 shows a remarkable shift (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) in campaign funding. Publicly financed candidates relied significantly more on small, in-district contributions than in past elections. Roughly twice as many (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) New Yorkers made small-dollar donations compared to the 2020 or 2022 cycles. The increase in small donations was driven by local constituents, which is striking in a state where out-of-district and out-of-state donors have historically dominated (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) election giving.
Other jurisdictions have had similar successes. In DC's (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/major-strides-public-campaign-financing) first citywide elections with public financing in 2020, publicly financed candidates tended to outraise and enjoy greater electoral success than their privately financed counterparts. In Seattle, the number of residents donating to city campaigns more than doubled (https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/EthicsElections/DemocracyVoucher/Program%20Data/Reports/2021%20Seattle%20Democracy%20Voucher%20Report.pdf?inline=1) in just the first few years that public financing was available. And after Berkeley, California's public financing program went into effect in 2018, contributions from non-Berkeley residents dropped (https://maplightarchive.org/story/2018-fair-elections-in-berkeley/) to 10 percent of total fundraising that year, down from 33 percent in 2016.
More on
Influence of Big Money (https://www.brennancenter.org/topics/money-politics/influence-big-money)
California (https://www.brennancenter.org/tags/california)
Proposition 4 comes at a critical time, both in California and nationally, when the public is profoundly angry (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) about the impact of wealth in American politics. A majority of Americans (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/09/poll-americans-say-too-much-money-in-politics-00912455) across the ideological spectrum say that there is too much money in politics. They're fed up with corruption in government and broadly support (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/poll-voters-want-solutions-government-corruption) major reforms to fix our campaign finance system. It's hardly surprising, then, that a recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/blog/commentary-affordability-is-the-top-issue-on-californias-november-ballot/) of California voters named threats to democracy as the most pertinent issue facing the country.
Americans across the country recognize the problem with the dominance of unchecked wealth in our elections. Proposition 4 presents Californians with an opportunity to shift course and build momentum for more ambitious change nationwide.

# GAO Publishes Report on Public Financing Programs
On December 19, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) published a **report** on public financing programs in selected states and localities.
The report, required by the 2023 federal appropriations bill, attempts to describe several key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities, such as grant funding, matching funds plans, voucher programs, and qualification and participation requirements.
The GAO also interviewed officials from nine programs to obtain perspectives on candidate participation and reasons for and for not participating in the programs.
Additionally, the report looks at the various legal frameworks of the programs and how observations of campaign financing programs in other states and localities influenced aspects of the respondents’ own program structures.
According to the report, which is relying on a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns.

- The committee’s use of matching funds for non-qualified campaign expenses (for example, the committee did not keep adequate records to document that their disbursements were made in connection with the primary campaign or the committee exceeded the expenditure limitations of 11 CFR 9035); and

Let me consolidate my analysis. I have a comprehensive picture. Let me weigh it.

**What Prop 4 actually does:**
- Repeals the 1988 Prop 73 ban on public campaign financing (Gov. Code § 85300), which currently bars the state, counties, general-law cities, and special districts (charter cities are exempt via Johnson v. Bradley, 1992).
- Does NOT create any program or appropriate any money. Direct state cost: a few hundred thousand dollars/year for FPPC legal staff (~$198k–205k/yr per FPPC).
- Sets guardrails: no education/transportation/public safety earmarked funds; candidates must accept spending limits and meet "strict criteria" (small-dollar support, max $10/donor counted, no signature or $ thresholds above $10/contributor); no public funds for legal defense, fines, or personal loan repayment (and a publicly funded candidate can never repay a personal loan from any source post-campaign); programs can't discriminate by party or incumbent/challenger status; a "rescue" clause allowing increased expenditure limits when outspent, capped by a formula.
- Triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign campaign contributions.
- FPPC explicitly NOT responsible for administering or enforcing local programs.
- Most of § 85300 can only be further amended by voters; definitions/spending-limit formula/FPPC clause amendable by 2/3 Legislature.

**Arguments for a YES:**
1. It's purely permissive — local control. It spends nothing and mandates nothing. Every jurisdiction that doesn't want public financing is entirely unaffected.
2. California is the only state with a statewide ban (accurate per supporters; 14-15 states + DC have programs, 26 localities).
3. Existing charter-city programs already do this; Prop 4 just removes an inequity between charter cities and general-law cities/counties/districts.
4. Real, documented benefits in well-designed programs: NYC 2021 most diverse council; Seattle democracy vouchers → donors doubled, +86% candidates, +4.9pp turnout (p=.085), low-income residents and people of color more likely to use vouchers; NY State 2024 → roughly 2x small donors, more in-district; Berkeley → out-of-town contributions fell from 33% to 10%; GAO 2024 found participating candidates generally won or advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 sites.
5. Broad good-government coalition: League of Women Voters, Common Cause, ACLU, CNA, Labor Federation, Brennan Center, Consumer Watchdog, SPUR, LA Times, McClatchy/Bee, Newsom, both legislative caucuses of Dems, and notably passed the Assembly 59–20 (some Republican support).
6. It has taxpayer guardrails written in and raises penalties on foreign money.
7. The counterweight to Citizens United: states can't cap independent expenditures by billionaires, but they can offer candidates an alternative funding source. In 2026 California saw $9M in outside spending on a single Assembly seat, and a $213M self-funded gubernatorial run.
8. Any actual program would still need to be approved by local voters/councils — an extra democratic checkpoint.

**Arguments for a NO:**
1. Politicians voting to unlock taxpayer money for their own campaigns — conflict of interest; the measure leaves all key design decisions (match rates, spending limits, budgets, eligibility thresholds) to the same people who benefit.
2. No enforcement mechanism: FPPC explicitly exempted from administering/enforcing local programs; no requirement that local governments create an independent ethics commission. SF Chronicle's central objection. Many general-law cities/counties have no watchdog.
3. Evidence is mixed on whether public financing actually reduces big-money influence: independent expenditures continue regardless (SF 2024: $8.84M public funds paid out, $19.0M outside spending — a record); Oakland 2013 study found "no evidence" of reduced wealthy-donor influence or increased turnout; GAO 2010 found no evidence of more candidates; LA's design found "substantially less effective" than NYC's in a 2017 peer-reviewed study; the presidential public financing system collapsed because caps didn't keep pace.
4. Cost: SF pays $8.8M in a single election cycle; LA pays participating mayoral candidates an average of $1.28M each. In a state with chronic deficits and 14 measures on the ballot (including an $11.25B housing bond), this creates a new open-ended category of government spending.
5. Fraud/abuse risk is real: NY State program saw federal prosecutions (Brian Benjamin, straw donors/homeless people used as fake donors, gift cards traded for donations, a candidate charged over $150k–$160k fraudulent matching funds, NYC Public Advocate candidate charged with wire fraud over $1M). California's measure has no independent auditor requirement.
6. Californians have rejected lifting this ban three times (2000: 34.7% yes; 2006: 25.7%; 2010: 42.7%), and the 1988 ban itself passed with 58%.
7. Polling: PPIC Sept 42–53, Oct 45–52; Berkeley IGS Sept 35–35 with 30% undecided, Oct 41–41 with 18% undecided. Independents oppose. Even with the Governor, Democratic Party, LA Times and McClatchy in favor, it can't reach 50%.
8. Editorial opposition from SF Chronicle, SD Union-Tribune, OC Register, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Press-Enterprise; Santa Cruz Sentinel neutral.

**My assessment:**

The key question: Is this a good policy change on the merits?

The measure itself is remarkably modest in direct effect — it appropriates nothing and mandates nothing. Its cost is a few hundred thousand dollars a year. If you think public financing of campaigns is a legitimate and effective tool, then this is a clear yes: it removes an anomalous, decades-old statewide prohibition and lets local communities decide, with reasonable guardrails built in and the option preserved for voters in each jurisdiction to say no again.

But the strongest objection is the one the SF Chronicle makes, and it's substantive: Prop 4 sets almost no substantive limits and explicitly removes the state's campaign-finance watchdog from local program enforcement, while handing all design decisions — match rates, spending caps, budgets — to legislators with a direct personal stake. In a state where local ethics enforcement is frequently weak (Inglewood's $100,000 contribution cap cited as an example), that's a genuine gap.

Weighing these:
- The "politicians funding themselves" concern is real but mitigated: any program still requires a separate affirmative vote by a city council, county board, or local electorate. That's a meaningful second checkpoint, and voters have consistently shown (three times statewide, and by defunding Oakland's program) that they're willing to say no.
- The "no oversight" concern is the strongest, but note that the FPPC still enforces the Political Reform Act's disclosure and contribution rules generally for local campaigns; what's exempted is administration/enforcement of the local public-funding system specifically. And jurisdictions creating programs can (and in practice do — SF, LA, Berkeley all have ethics commissions) set up oversight. It's a design choice left open, not a prohibition.
- The effectiveness evidence is mixed but leans positive for well-designed small-donor matching programs (NYC/NYS, Seattle, Berkeley). The failures (LA's design, the federal system, Oakland's) are design failures, and the design question remains with localities.
- On cost: public financing is cheap relative to the money already flowing. SF spends $2.75/resident/year; supporters say as little as $1/resident/year. Compare $8.84M in SF public funds to $19M in outside spending — but that $19M is exactly the money public financing aims to counterbalance, and it can't be capped under Citizens United. Doing nothing guarantees the billionaire-dominated status quo.

The decisive consideration for me: This is a permissive, local-control measure with real guardrails (no education/transportation/public-safety money, spending limits mandatory, small-donor qualification mandatory, no incumbent/party favoritism, no legal-defense/fines/personal-loan repayment, tripled foreign-money penalties) that costs the state almost nothing directly and creates no program. It removes an outdated, uniquely Californian prohibition that has produced an inconsistency — charter cities like SF, LA, Berkeley can do it while a general-law city or a county cannot. And critically, the actual spending decision remains with local voters and councils, who can reject any program.

The opposition's core claim — "NO LIMIT on the number of candidates" / "NO LIMIT on how much" — is technically true of the measure's text but misleading: the measure *requires* expenditure limits on participating candidates and requires small-donor qualification; it simply lets each locality set the numbers, which is appropriate for a local-control measure. And their claim that it "allows special interest money in politics" is a non-sequitur — special-interest money is already allowed; public financing adds an alternative, not a new source.

The genuinely serious objection (no mandated independent oversight of local programs) is a real drafting flaw, but it isn't disqualifying, since jurisdictions must still build their own programs and most that have done so created ethics commissions.

Also relevant: the measure is endorsed by the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, ACLU, Brennan Center, SPUR, LA Times, McClatchy papers — the state's most credible good-government institutions — and was placed on the ballot by a bipartisan-ish supermajority (Assembly 59–20, Senate 29–8).

So my recommendation: YES.

Let me do one more sanity check on whether there's any hidden trap — e.g., does it allow public funding for county central committee candidates (opponents claim)? "Public funds" = "any moneys provided to a candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the purpose of seeking elective office." County central committee members are elected in partisan primaries under the Elections Code — they are elective offices. So technically yes, a county could fund those races, though it's unlikely and would require the county to affirmatively choose to. Not disqualifying.

Also: could the state Legislature create a statewide program for itself with a simple majority? Yes, by statute. That's the biggest self-dealing risk. But again, that would be a separate, visible legislative act subject to public scrutiny and electoral accountability — and California's legislature has repeatedly failed to fund even modest programs (Oakland's is unfunded).

One more consideration: the measure's fiscal responsibility framing. Given the state has been running large deficits and has an $11.25B housing bond on the same ballot, does adding a new potential spending category matter? The LAO says the direct cost is trivial and any program cost depends on future decisions. So no.

I'm fairly confident: YES. The measure is permissive, cheap, well-guardrailed, supported by the state's leading good-government organizations, removes a unique-in-the-nation ban, and leaves every actual spending decision to future local/state votes.
